entries.test: NVIDIA's customer concentration disclosures, rack pricing, customer purchasing capacity and counterparties' financing records would test the asserted revenue concentration and financing dependence.
entries.note: The central assertion explains NVIDIA's dependence on customers and debt. The tentative identification of those customers is an incidental hedge.

entries.test: Hyperscalers' equity issuance, borrowing terms, credit availability and public financing disclosures would show whether equity sales coincide with increasing difficulty obtaining debt.
entries.note: He adopts Kedrosky's point in his own declarative statement.

entries.test: Public revenue figures, compute spending and infrastructure financial requirements would test whether the stated 2030 compute-demand level requires roughly $400 billion in annual revenue from each company.
entries.note: 'Both ... about $400 billion a year' does not clearly commit to $400 billion between them. The normalization resolves that ambiguity without sufficient support.

entries.test: Microsoft's disclosed AI revenue composition would show whether OpenAI compute accounts for most of its $37 billion annual run rate and Copilot accounts for the remainder.
entries.note: The revenue-composition assertion is firm; the $8 billion estimate is explicitly tentative.
'AI stories' has no shared criterion: it could mean products, strategy, revenue or investor narratives.

entries.test: Public customer retention, renewals, spending and provider financial results would test whether AI revenue collected without advance cost visibility can persist sustainably.
entries.note: The categorical economic assertion has a testable plain reading despite the accompanying insults.

entries.test: Public examples of LLM outputs beyond apps and representative evidence of generated apps' usage, utility and security would test the exclusivity and majority claims.
entries.note: The insults accompany factual assertions about output scope and the prevalence of unusable or insecure apps.
The bundled claim includes explicitly 'very likely' billing and subscription changes. Its separate prediction of inevitable price increases is firm and checkable.
The central claim attributes a private desire and deliberate motive to AI labs. Public money flows alone cannot establish that motive.
This is a hypothetical causal chain about what demand would be under an alternative corporate objective. It requires a counterfactual comparison.

entries.test: Public releases, independently measured customer ROI and disclosed operating costs and compute spending would test whether labs possess the asserted breakthrough or cost-reduction capability.
entries.note: The normalization broadens 'some magical way' into 'any way,' potentially excluding ordinary cost reductions that the source does not clearly rule out.
